Watch who follows, makes space, greets, rests or gives a gentle shove. These habits come from inherited traits. Watch the tank to discover their personalities. Arrange leaves, bark tunnels and stones. Watch antennae sweep, legs tuck at rest and front legs groom. Favorite places are learned through visits and saved with the tank. Hover over a beetle for its current activity. Open Familiar neighbors & little moments to follow relationships and rare events.

How their bodies and traits shape behavior

Longer antennae extend nearby detection. Body size sets clearance and resistance to nudges. Leg length contributes to speed; leg spread, feet and grip affect footing near stones. Curious beetles investigate; cautious beetles prefer bark cover. Sociality guides greetings, while endurance and recovery shape rest. Favorite places are learned, rather than inherited. These are invented teaching rules.

    THE POCKET FIELD GUIDE
    Make the beetle you imagine.
    Choose, breed, discover
    Click a beetle for a large view, then add it to a jar. You can also drag a tank beetle into a jar slot. Put two to four different beetles in a jar, check “Use this jar,” and breed. One jar produces 10–20 babies. Two jars split that same total; an odd extra goes randomly to either. Each baby gets two distinct parents chosen randomly inside its own jar. Two parents in a jar keep that cross exclusive. Original parents stay until you remove them.
    A quiet, living tank
    Beetles wander after birth. Drag a beetle to place it. Holding pauses only that beetle; opening its information leaves the others moving. Cool & pause freezes both tanks with a brief pretend mist; Run resumes movement. Cooling, bedding, decoration and movement do not change genes or breeding chances. There are no birds, hunger or automatic mating. The optional sumo table is a harmless pushing contest. Inherited speed changes walking pace, while strength is a fictional relative trait, not a fertility advantage. The short field-mark tags are consistent clues; discover their meaning through observation and breeding. In sumo, muscle force drives a sustained push; speed helps approaching and circling. Every trait has its own role. Strength supplies muscle force; grip transfers it, stamina preserves energy, recovery restores spent energy and clears disruption, and behavior and position determine when a push works. Compare beetles shows force, traction, speed, turning and all adaptation factors. Full-stat matches display remaining energy and current applied push. Factors requiring missing anatomy are marked clearly. Read How traits affect the match for the complete 110-record audit.
    Flipping and getting back up
    More effective horn lifts have higher chances of flipping the other beetle. Horn reach, lift power and control help; the opponent’s mass, grip and balance resist. A successful lift can still stop short of a flip. Upside-down beetles cannot push or use special moves and offer much less resistance until they right themselves. Recovery, legs and body build affect the time. A brief grace period after righting prevents an immediate chain of flips. These are harmless game rules; no beetle loses genes or gets hurt.
    Lift, spring, puff
    Horn lifts, spring jumps and cartoon bombardier puffs happen automatically during sumo when a beetle has the anatomy and instinct. A lift has to get underneath from the front; grip, bracing, a low body and a side approach can counter it. A jump escapes contact but cannot push in the air; poor landing control can send it out. A puff briefly disrupts aim and pushing, with only two charges per match. It can miss or be dodged by jumping. Watch the wind-up: each attempt costs energy and leaves time to respond. Power, reach, control, efficiency, recovery and instinct breed gradually for each move. Spring joints and puff glands are very rare recessive structures; hidden carriers can produce a surprise. A selected family can retain them. These are invented, harmless grappling rules. Ring-outs and the center tiebreak still decide matches; everyone recovers fully afterward.
    Genes that can hide
    The model stores 113 paired records on eleven chromosome pairs. Colors, markings, finish and categorical forms have two inherited copies. Continuous anatomy and behavior are breeding-value estimates representing many small genetic effects. A baby gets a contribution from each actual parent. Color, pattern and categorical forms transmit actual parental copies, including hidden variants. Overall body size combines inherited length and width as a continuous measurement, without small/medium/large tiers. Students can track it in the raw data notebook. Size dimensions, speed-related values, stamina, strength, continuous appendage dimensions, and behavior usually stay close to the parents’ averages, with small variation in either direction. Rare larger mutations can make a bigger change. Linked copies usually travel together; a crossover can exchange sections. A dominant S suppressor hides marks. Only ss reveals them; a separate T gate limits visible patterns to one color, while tt allows two. Both hidden colors and placement genes still pass on. Two Ss Tt parents with mutation off can produce plain, one-color and two-color offspring. Small broods need not match average odds.
    One hundred ten inherited records
    Body and pattern colors, mark size and distribution, symmetry, antenna frameworks, fine hairs, leg forms, motor speed and strength all have their own inherited copies. Frameworks can mask modifiers. Continuous physical and behavior traits use a quantitative breeding model, so they do not flip between a parent’s widely different hidden values. Colors and pattern genes can still reveal inherited surprises. The stronger expression copy selects a categorical framework or pigment recipe; numeric copies average when expressed. Quantitative contributions are formed near each parent’s expressed value before mutation, rather than choosing a single large-effect allele. No antenna or color is universally better. Stable developmental variation gives each baby a fixed pattern; inspecting, cooling or resizing never rerolls it.
    From tiny to extravagant
    Antennae include threads, beads, bristles, clubs, sawteeth, single and double combs, fans, leaf plates, elbows, plumes and side bristles. Length, width, segments, branching, fine hair and spread vary too. These mix beetle and other insect inspirations for creative play; they are not a species identification tool. Legs keep three pairs and can show runners, sturdy walkers, shovel forelegs, large hind thighs, paddles, hooks, spines and long toes.
    Growing a distinctive build
    New founders begin with horn nubs. Select offspring with longer horns to grow them over generations. Body size, antennae, legs, head, jaws and horns have gradual proportional growth modifiers. Very rare framework mutations can introduce curved or forked horns, and double horns; triple horns can arise from a double-horn line. Once inherited, these discoveries can become common in a selected family. Large bodies gain push resistance but lose speed and turning agility. Long appendages bring smaller contest tradeoffs. The sumo table compresses extreme body-size differences to keep the ring playable.
    Legs and thorax each have their own paired pigment genes, separate from the shell. Hidden pigments can reappear in a later baby. Leg and thorax colors have the same inherited brightness modifier as other appendages; no color wins sumo automatically.
    Personality in the tank
    Inherited sociability makes approaching and greeting more likely. Cautious beetles prefer personal space and slower turns near walls. Curious beetles investigate new places; wandering, focus and persistence change their paths and how long they follow. Push-driven beetles may give a brief gentle shove, then separate and cool down. Strength and mass affect that small nudge. Endurance and recovery affect activity and rest. Watch the temporary activity labels or hover for the current action. Beetles also visit food and water dishes and a warm light spot as their hunger, thirst and comfort change. Supplies are unlimited and no beetle can starve, dehydrate or overheat. Appetite, thirst drive and warmth preference are inherited gradually and affect visit frequency; warmth preference also affects basking time. Focus helps remember an unfinished food, water or warmth task after being moved or interrupted. Low-focus beetles can get distracted first. New arrivals bring varied habitat genes; older saved beetles start at neutral values. Choose these traits in the magnifier, simple report or raw-data notebook to compare descendants. The same behavior and dishes work in Keep. Holding stops only that beetle, cooling pauses everyone, and inspecting does not stop the tank. These are invented game behaviors: no injuries, automatic breeding, gene changes or lost beetles occur.
    Keep a family
    The tank holds at most 48 beetles. Choose whether tank and nursery keep the newest brood only or the two newest broods; the starting group counts as a brood. A change takes effect when the next brood is born. Older unsaved beetles then leave automatically, while their trait measurements remain in the notebook. Keep up to ten favorites in the separate top-down Keep tank, return others to the breeder tank, and select descendants for later crosses. Save favorites before the next brood arrives. Keep tank beetles and jar parents are protected. The magnifying-glass button opens a dense technical report with all 113 paired genetic records, both copies, full-precision expression values, mutation flags, expression gates and derived size/speed measurements. Teacher labs can always open it. In student links it follows Show all genetics. The report can be downloaded or printed. Simple trait report brings back the familiar horizontal bars for movement, build and behavior, without the chromosome tables. It follows the same genetics visibility permission; the student raw-data notebook remains a table. Named beetles are automatically excluded from cleanup. Their names appear on hover and in the inspector. Inspect a beetle to toggle Exclude from cleanup. Exclusions stay with the saved tank, are not inherited, and do not use a Keep tank slot. Clear unsaved beetles opens a review list; check exclusions and confirm which beetles to delete. Cancel changes nothing. Family labels, portraits and measured trait data remain after deletion. Older archived beetles without a saved portrait are marked appearance not recorded. Brood rounds count crossings; lineage generation follows actual ancestry. Repeated broods of the same parents are siblings.
    Meet new arrivals
    Beetle store displays five random beetles. Choose up to two per breeding round, using appearance alone. Hidden genes and statistics are never shown in the store, including in full-stat classes. Five new arrivals replace the selection after a successful breeding round. Reopening or reloading keeps the current selection and picks. Store arrivals join the tank, or nursery if the tank is full, and follow normal cleanup rules. Keep favorites safe before breeding.
    Trade with a classmate
    Choose a beetle outside the jars and create a trade code. Your friend enters the code and offers a beetle back. Preview both, then the code creator confirms sharing. Both students keep their original and get an exact copy of the other beetle. Either student can cancel first. Keep using the original tank and device until finished. Trades need internet and device storage. Codes for the sumo table are separate; battles never move your beetles.
    Compare three traits quickly
    Below the breeder tank, turn on Trait magnifier and search the three trait boxes. Hover over beetles to see a small portrait card with those readings while the tank continues moving. The card switches as you point at another beetle and closes when you leave the tank. It also works in the Keep tank, with occupied parent jars and with keyboard focus. Full-stat links and teacher labs can choose extra expressed factors; other student links retain the measurable notebook traits and visible forms, with strength and hidden copies excluded.
    Collect trait data
    Open the trait notebook to choose a measurement such as walking speed, stamina or antenna length. Read the raw data table across lineage generations or breeding rounds, filter by jar, and download the selected individual measurements as CSV. Archived measurements remain after beetles leave the tank; older missing records are marked unavailable. Strength and hidden gene copies are excluded from the notebook even when full statistics are enabled.
    Save your work
    The lab auto-saves locally when available and automatically reopens your last tank for this class link on this browser and device. New tank is a separate, confirmed choice. Different class links have separate saves. Save tank file downloads a portable copy including all genes, jar groups, names and notes. Open tank file restores it. Shared class links start a fresh tank with the same founders and permissions; they do not contain your later offspring. On shared school devices, save a file before leaving. This original model teaches inheritance and is not a claim about actual beetle genetics.

    OBSERVE, THEN BREED AGAIN
    The match notebook
    YOUR FIELD GUIDE
    Beetle lab FAQ
    Rules, controls and the explanations behind your beetles. Your lab stays open in its original tab.
    Battle rulesFriend battlesBehavior summaryCleanupSharingBreedingTrait reference
    How do battles work?
    Push the other beetle’s center over the white line to win immediately. At 60 seconds, the beetle closest to the center wins; only an equal-distance finish is a tie. If both cross the line in the same instant, the closer beetle wins. The circles are distance guides, not separate point zones. Playback speed changes the animation, not the result.
    No beetle is injured or lost. A battle does not change its inherited traits. Its corner caption describes its current behavior.
    How do horns, spring jumps, puffs and tactics help?
    Lift · spring · puff
    Horn lifts can loosen grip or flip an opponent. Missing horns cannot lift or flip; tiny nubs have very little leverage. Longer functional horns and higher lifts raise the flip chance; upside-down beetles are easier to push until they recover. Rare spring joints let a beetle hop; rare puff glands briefly scramble aim. Watch the wind-up. Each move spends energy and needs time to recover. There are two puffs per match.
    A front push meets bracing. Side pushes test sideways balance; rear pushes test recovery. Mass and grip resist sliding, but a heavy beetle accelerates and turns more slowly.
    Tracking, reaction speed, focus and ring tactics help find a useful angle. Pushing and wandering instincts can pull in opposite directions. Endurance matters in a long contest.
    How do I battle a friend on another computer?
    1. Each person opens their own lab and chooses a beetle from Your beetle for this table.
    2. The host chooses a shared speed and clicks Create table with this beetle, then shares the code.
    3. The friend enters that code and clicks the large Send beetle to table button.
    4. When both beetles are present, the host clicks Start friend battle below the ring.
    The host chooses 2× or 10× speed for both screens. The countdown and victory dance stay at normal speed. Both screens use the same moves and winner. Keep both pages open; returning screens catch up. Codes expire after two hours. Only the chosen beetle’s anonymous genetic packet is sent. Your original stays in your tank.
    What do the post-battle counts and seconds mean?
    After a battle ends, open Battle behavior summary below the result. It lists the 17 current behavior labels separately for red and blue. A count increases each time a beetle enters that behavior. Seconds measure time spent in that displayed state using battle time. Playing at 10× does not change the counts or duration.
    Copy the summary or download its CSV to share. The dropdown clears when another battle or rematch starts. Your latest completed summary stays shareable while you choose the next opponent. New saved battle records keep these measurements; older matches can generate a summary when replayed.
    How does automatic tank cleanup work?
    The cleanup dropdown beside Breed selected jars chooses whether to keep the newest brood or the two newest broods in the tank and nursery when the next brood arrives. Save favorites in the Keep tank before breeding. Keep favorites, jar parents, pending trades and beetles excluded from cleanup remain protected. The Keep tank holds ten beetles.
    Tank replacement normally unlocks after five successful breeding cycles. The separate starter-recovery option can add beetles when the working tank is empty or too few beetles remain to breed. Saved beetle snapshots can recover earlier specimens.
    How does sharing differ from a battle?
    Sharing makes a genetic copy for each student; both keep their original beetle. Choose an eligible beetle, create a sharing code, and have your friend join with one of theirs. The code creator confirms the exchange. Keep the original tank on the same browser and device until it finishes. Open offers expire in two hours; completed exchanges can be collected for seven days.
    A friend battle does not move either beetle. After a completed battle, each person may copy the opponent to their own tank. A full tank sends incoming beetles to Nursery.
    How do the parent jars divide a brood?
    Choose two to four parents for each active jar. Each baby gets two distinct parents from its own jar. One complete jar produces all 10–20 babies; two complete jars split the brood. Keep two parents in a jar for an exclusive cross. Incomplete jars are skipped. The birth confirmation remains visible after breeding.

    What does each battle trait affect?
    Strength breeding value
    Muscle force in a sustained push. Strength 1 produces 100 times the base force of 0.01. Grip, remaining energy and facing determine how much reaches the opponent.
    Opponent tracking
    How accurately a beetle aims at a moving opponent.
    Reaction speed
    How often it reconsiders its direction.
    Attention focus
    How reliably it keeps attending to its opponent.
    Pushing instinct
    The tendency to approach and push instead of exploring.
    Wandering instinct
    The tendency to choose a wandering path. It can interrupt a promising push.
    Turning agility
    How quickly it turns. High mass and very fast running make sharp turns harder.
    Ring tactics (game intelligence)
    Game intelligence: predicts movement and sometimes circles toward the inside of the ring before pushing outward.
    Edge awareness
    How early and reliably it notices the boundary and aims back toward the center. Strong pushes can still carry it out.
    Bracing instinct
    How firmly it supports a head-on push. Settling into a brace also slows turning during contact.
    Sideways balance
    Resistance to being moved by a side push.
    Foot grip
    How effectively feet transfer force to the table. It helps pushing and resisting a shove.
    Endurance
    How slowly pushing effort drains its available energy.
    Recovery
    How quickly it recovers from a lift, puff or awkward landing, regains energy between efforts and away from contact, and rights itself after a flip. It also helps resist rear pushes.
    Body mass
    Heavier beetles resist changes in movement and off-center shoves, but accelerate and turn more slowly.
    Acceleration
    How quickly it builds up walking speed.
    Center preference
    How strongly exploratory paths favor the middle.
    Curiosity
    How often exploration turns into investigating the opponent’s projected path. It changes wandering directions and approach choices.
    Social approach
    How often an exploring beetle approaches another beetle, in the tank and across the sumo ring. It changes approach paths, not muscle force.
    Caution
    How much it slows an outward walk near the boundary. Edge awareness decides when to turn inward; caution controls the risky pace.
    Persistence
    How likely it is to keep pursuing an ongoing push.
    Horn lift · power
    Lift strength combines horn reach and positioning. A wind-up weakens pushing; a lift briefly reduces the other beetle’s grip. A higher lift has a greater chance of flipping the opponent. Flipped beetles cannot push and have low resistance until they right themselves; recovery, legs and body build affect that time. Short horns, low bodies, strong grip and bracing reduce its effect. Side approaches can make it miss.
    Spring jump · power
    A spring joint must be inherited to jump. Jumps can escape a lift or puff; the beetle cannot push while airborne. Landing control, edge awareness and stamina matter. A risky jump can go out of bounds.
    Bombardier puff · power
    A puff gland must be inherited. Two cartoon puffs per match can briefly scramble an opponent’s aim and pushing. Range and facing matter; jumping can dodge a puff. Both charges return in the next match. These are invented harmless game rules.
    Horn lift · reach
    How much leverage an existing horn supplies.
    Horn lift · aim / landing control
    Accuracy and control for horn lift. Improves aim or landing and shortens the wind-up.
    Horn lift · efficiency
    How little energy this move spends. The lowest efficiency costs five times the energy of the highest.
    Horn lift · recovery speed
    How soon this move is ready again. The lowest recovery takes four times as long as the highest.
    Horn lift · use instinct
    How often this beetle attempts the move when anatomy, position, energy and cooldown allow it.
    Spring jump · reach
    How far an expressed spring joint carries a hop.
    Spring jump · aim / landing control
    Accuracy and control for spring jump. Improves aim or landing and shortens the wind-up.

    How little energy this move spends. The lowest efficiency costs five times the energy of the highest.

    How soon this move is ready again. The lowest recovery takes four times as long as the highest.

    How far an expressed puff gland can reach.
